name: Akumal
label: Akumal Bay
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Half Moon Bay' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Half Moon Bay Condos' (node/6303183420): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Bay known for swimming with sea turtles.

text.description:
Akumal is a small beach resort village on the Caribbean coast of Quintana Roo, about 100 km south of Cancún and between Playa del Carmen and Tulum. It began in 1958 as a community for scuba divers, on the site of a former coconut plantation. Today it is best known for snorkelling, because green sea turtles come into the bay to feed on sea grass. Akumal Bay was declared a marine refuge in 2016 to protect them. The main bay can be busy, so this spot suggests Half Moon Bay, a quieter bay nearby that you reach on foot from the shore.

It photographs well because the reef keeps the water calm and turquoise, and the shoreline makes a clean, simple edge to the frame. Half Moon Bay gives you the colour of the water without the crowds of the main beach. You can come away with pictures that look different from the usual Akumal shots. If you are in the main bay too, a wider view across the water with the beach and palms is a good second picture.

For a phone, keep the horizon level and let the water colour carry the shot. Wipe the lens first, as sea spray and sunscreen smear it easily. Keep your distance from any turtles and wildlife, and take pictures of them from the shore or from a respectful distance rather than getting close.
text.geographic_location: Akumal is in Tulum Municipality, Quintana Roo, on the Riviera Maya coast between Playa del Carmen and the town of Tulum. Half Moon Bay is the quieter bay next to the main Akumal Bay.
text.directions_text: Akumal lies on the coast between Playa del Carmen and Tulum, so check local transport options for getting there. Once in Akumal, head for Half Moon Bay on foot along the shore. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the bay, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a distant swimmer or a line of palms.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (quieter bay near Akumal, reached on foot from shore). Reef-protected turquoise water and the shoreline of a quieter bay, as a quieter alternative to the main beach.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line so the water fills most of the frame. Include a strip of sand in the foreground for depth. If you also visit Akumal Bay, try a wider view of the beach and calm water there as a second picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest patch of water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white sand does not wash out and the turquoise stays rich. Keep your phone dry and clean the lens before shooting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check conditions on the day, as seaweed can sometimes collect along the shore.

text.access_note: Akumal Bay is a marine refuge and rules at the beaches can change, so check local guidance or the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Seaweed (sargassum) can collect along the shore at some times of year.
Sea spray and sunscreen can smear a phone lens.
Rules for beach access and wildlife in the marine refuge may change.

name: Tulum Archaeological Site
label: Tulum Ruins
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'El Castillo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'El Castillo' (way/160485979): middle (55 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16824245: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tulum Archaeological Zone' (545 m across).
notes: Walled Maya port city on a cliff above the Caribbean.

text.description: Tulum was a walled Maya port city on 12-metre cliffs above the Caribbean, and El Castillo, the site's best-known building, is the photograph most visitors come for. The city reached its greatest prominence between the 13th and 15th centuries and was abandoned by the end of the 16th. It photographs well because the stone temple sits right on the cliff edge with turquoise water behind it, so one frame gives you history and sea together. The site was protected on the landward side by a wall averaging 3-5 metres high and about 8 metres thick. In 1843 the explorers Stephens and Catherwood arrived by sea and were struck by a tall building, most likely El Castillo. Go early: the morning light falls on the main face and there are fewer tour groups to dodge. If you have time, two other views are worth a look: Playa Ruinas, for the cliff-top temples above the beach and surf, and the Templo del Dios del Viento, a small round-based temple on the cliff. Beach access depends on conditions and tides.
text.geographic_location: On the Caribbean coast of Quintana Roo, on the cliffs at the edge of the Tulum Archaeological Zone, a walled Maya site about 545 metres across.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, and no public transport stops are listed either, so check local options for reaching the archaeological site. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the cliff, the sea and, if you turn back along the cliff, the ruins all fit in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the paths are busy and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the temple's top and doorways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (east-facing base of the pyramid, looking out over the water). The main temple on its cliff edge with the turquoise Caribbean filling the background. From here the sea is the view ahead. For the temple on its cliff edge, turn and shoot back along the cliff. The middle of the walled site lies to the west of this point, so the other ruins are on the landward side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, keeping it level. Leave a little sky above the ruins so the frame does not look cramped. For a different view, Playa Ruinas gives a cove-style shot of the cliff-top temples above the surf.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the temple to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sea stays blue and does not wash out. Try a Live Photo for waves and moving people. Use portrait mode only for a friend standing in front, not for the ruins themselves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: 8-9 AM, when the morning light hits the main face of the temple and there are fewer tour groups in the frame.

text.access_note: This is a protected archaeological site that is likely to have entry rules, so check the official site (INAH) for entry fees, camera, tripod and drone rules and beach access before you go.

name: Gran Cenote
label: Gran Cenote
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gran Cenote' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N976101133 (Gran Cenote): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Popular clear-water cenote for swimming and snorkelling.

text.description:
Gran Cenote is a natural swimming spot in the Tulum area, where clear turquoise water sits in a cave setting with soft cave light. That mix of turquoise water, rock and soft light is why it photographs so well on a phone. The main area is the busiest part, so the quieter corners are the best places to take your time.

For a calmer picture, head to the smaller area to the right of the cenote stairs, or to the second sinkhole further into the cave. Guides describe these as less crowded than the main area. They show a quieter pool against the cave backdrop, with fewer people in the frame. From the wooden platform you can also look down into the pool and see the turquoise water and the cave light. A view from above shows the clear water and the open pool as a whole.

Guides report that tripods and cameras are not allowed, but phone photos and GoPros are, and that visitors must shower before getting in. Rules and entry details can change, so check the current rules on the day. Take a moment to wipe your lens, as the air around the water can be damp. Then try one wide shot of the whole scene and one closer shot of the water and rock.
text.geographic_location: Gran Cenote is in the Tulum area of Mexico.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Use your map app to get to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the pool and cave together, especially from the wooden platform. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the water and the cave opening. Use 2x or the telephoto if your phone has one, for details such as light on the water or rock shapes, without walking into other people's shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the quieter picture, go to the smaller area to the right of the cenote stairs, or to the second sinkhole further into the cave. From there you see a calmer pool against the cave backdrop, with fewer people in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on the lower line, with the cave roof filling the top third. Keep the horizon level, because curved rock can make a tilted shot look odd. If the main area is busy, move to the quieter section. If you want the classic view instead, the wooden platform looking down into the turquoise pool is the other recommended spot, and a view from above shows the open pool as a whole.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the water to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the light areas keep their colour. If the shot is too dark inside the cave, tap a shadowed area and lift the exposure slightly. Try a Live Photo to catch ripples, and wipe the lens before shooting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: I can't give a specific best time. Visit when it's quieter, and look at the light in the cave as you arrive, since it changes through the day.

text.access_note: This is a paid-entry site with rules about showering and what equipment you can bring, so check the current rules on the day.

name: Dos Ojos
label: Dos Ojos
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cenote Dos Ojos' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1273902: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Twin-eyed cave system famous for diving and snorkelling.

text.description:
Dos Ojos means 'Two Eyes', and the name fits. Two neighbouring cenotes (natural sinkholes) open into one large shared cavern, and they appear like two large eyes into the underground. The water is very clear because rainwater is filtered through pure limestone, and it stays at about 25 °C all year. Near the cenotes it is only around 10 metres deep, so the turquoise colour is easy to see. The cave system beneath is part of a huge flooded network that has been explored since 1987, and it has appeared in the BBC series Planet Earth.

For photographs, the appeal is the contrast between dark rock and glowing blue water. The first (east) eye is the classic view, with clear water and a bright cavern entrance. The second (west) eye is reached through the gallery from the first. It is darker and more dramatic, with long stalactites hanging over the turquoise pool. Both are worth a few frames if the crowds allow.

The cavern is dim and the light varies a lot between the openings and the shadows, so take a moment over each shot. Check the official site before you go for entry arrangements and any rules on photography.
text.geographic_location: Dos Ojos is a cenote and cave system on the Caribbean coast of the Yucatán Peninsula in Quintana Roo, about 20 km north of Tulum town.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby, so start from Tulum town and head north along Highway 307 for about 20 km. The cenote park is on that main road. Once inside, follow the paths to the first eye and then through the gallery to the second. Check the official site before you go for the latest access details. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the cavern opening, the water and the rock around it. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the water and the boardwalk. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), it suits close shots of individual stalactites and ripples in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the more dramatic picture, go through the gallery from the first eye to the second (west) eye. From there you can photograph the darker, more imposing cave, with long stalactites hanging from the ceiling above the turquoise water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water in the lower third, with the stalactites and cave ceiling filling the top. The wide view of the second eye works well with the ceiling as a frame around the blue. As an alternative, shoot the east eye from the wooden boardwalk where visitors step into the water, showing the clear blue water and the cavern entrance. Wait a moment for people to move out of the shot if you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright water or the opening, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the blues stay rich and are not washed out. In the darker parts of the cave, try night mode, and brace your elbows against a rail or your body to keep still while it works. Live Photos can catch ripples on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The cavern is crowded at weekends, so a weekday visit may be easier, with fewer people in the water. Check the official site before you go for current hours and conditions.

text.access_note: Dos Ojos is a managed park and cenote that may be ticketed, with its own rules on photography, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A weekday visit may be easier than a weekend.
Brightness inside the cavern varies sharply between the openings and the shadowed areas.
Leaning on a rail or bracing the elbows helps keep a phone steady in night mode.

name: Temple of the Frescoes
label: Temple of Frescoes
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Templo de los Frescos' (5 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W160485995 (Temple of the Frescoes): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Small painted temple inside the Tulum archaeological site.

text.description: The Temple of the Frescoes sits right in front of El Castillo inside the Tulum archaeological zone. That is what makes it work for a phone photo. You get a close, detailed subject in front and the larger, more recognisable building behind it, so the picture says 'Tulum' without any caption. The outer walls carry stucco figures and corner masks, and these give your foreground plenty of texture. The painted murals inside are closed to visitors to protect them, so this is an outside-only photo, and it is the standard shot that guides describe for this area. Head for the phone icon on the map, which marks the temple itself, then step back to the southeast side, face the front of the temple and keep El Castillo beside it in the frame. Try one wide shot that shows both buildings, then step in for a tighter picture of the stucco figures and masks. Entry to the archaeological zone is required, so check the official site before you go for current rules. Flash is discouraged near the frescoes, so switch it off. Going early, soon after opening, usually gives better light and fewer people walking through your frame. If you're staying later, one guide suggests the west-facing side for warmer late-day light.
text.geographic_location: Inside the Tulum archaeological zone, directly in front of El Castillo.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops nearby, so from Tulum town go to the archaeological zone by taxi or hired scooter. Once you are through the entrance, walk to El Castillo; the Temple of the Frescoes sits in front of it. Follow the phone icon on the map to the temple, then step back to the southeast side to frame it with El Castillo. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the temple and El Castillo both fit and look natural. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people or ropes force you to stand close. Use 2x or 3x telephoto, if your phone has it, for the stucco figures and corner masks.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the outer stucco figures and corner masks, with El Castillo behind them for context.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the temple on the lower third, leaving El Castillo in the upper background. Keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Then take a second, closer frame of the stucco figures or a corner mask. Wait a moment for people to move out of the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the temple to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework stays detailed. Turn the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, right after opening, when the light is better and there are fewer people. For warm late-day light, one guide suggests the west-facing side.

text.access_note: Entry to the Tulum archaeological zone is required and the temple's interior is closed to visitors, so photograph from outside only and check the official site before you go.

name: Xel-Há
label: Xel-Há
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Floating bridge' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Floating Bridge' (way/272537665): middle (67 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1526776: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Natural lagoon and eco park north of Tulum.

text.description: Xel-Há sits on a lagoon and inlet on the eastern coast of the Yucatán Peninsula, and the name comes from Yucatec Maya words for "spring" and "water". Long before it became a water park, it was a Maya settlement, occupied by the 1st century and active through Classic and Postclassic times. It served as one of the ports of the Maya city of Coba, alongside Tancah and Tulum. In 1527 the Spanish conquistador Francisco de Montejo landed at these lagoons and tried to found a settlement here. It failed, and the camp was abandoned within about eighteen months. Today the lagoon is part of Xel-Ha Park, so what you photograph is mostly water, jungle and walkways. The recommended viewpoint for a phone is the floating bridge. It crosses the snorkelling lagoon and looks out over turquoise water edged with jungle trees. It sits low, so the water fills the foreground and the trees frame both sides. Take a few shots along the walkway, then one with the bridge rail leading into the frame. If you want a different angle, the park also has a lighthouse tower with a wide view over the jungle and coast, and Cenote Paraiso, a freshwater cenote with a bridge across it. Both are inside the park.
text.geographic_location: Xel-Há is on the Caribbean coast of Quintana Roo, south of Playa del Carmen and on the Tulum map, on a lagoon and inlet that now form Xel-Ha Park.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop nearby, so follow the map to the park entrance. Once inside, follow the walkways to the floating bridge over the snorkelling lagoon, the recommended viewpoint. Check the park's official site before you go for entry arrangements. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole lagoon and the trees along its edges. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a distant stretch of shoreline or people snorkelling.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Floating bridge (across the snorkelling lagoon, shooting over the water). The turquoise snorkelling lagoon stretching out from the walkway, with the jungle trees along its edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, with plenty of water in the foreground. Let the bridge rail lead the eye into the frame. For a higher view, the lighthouse is an alternative; for a framed cenote scene, try Cenote Paraiso. Both are inside the park, so check the official site before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the trees to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright water keeps its colour. Hold the phone firmly with both hands over the water, and consider a wrist strap.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the park's official site for opening times and likely crowds before you go. Fewer people in the shot makes for a cleaner photo.

text.access_note: Xel-Há is a paid park, so the floating bridge needs park admission; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Lowering the exposure slider helps keep bright water from washing out in a phone photo.
The lighthouse tower and the cenote are both inside the park.
The floating bridge's exact position relative to the stand-here point is not confirmed.
